correctness.rationale: For every typed finite bipartite input, a synchronous Z-rule step concatenates three old cross-shore walks. Inductively every odd original shortest-path length at most \(3^{t+1}\) can be partitioned into three positive odd lengths at most \(3^t\), proving the exact trajectory. Opposite-shore shortest simple paths use equally many vertices from each part, giving maximum distance \(2\min(p,q)-1\); alternating paths attain equality. Counting odd-distance pairs on the path gives \(J_t(2h-J_t)\). For the historically distinct anchored relation update, the fixed outer edges give radius \(2t+1\) by a separate induction. Reproduction code directly compared old-edge completion and independently computed BFS distances in 71,642 incidence matrices and 25 extremal paths; finite checking is not substituted for the all-size induction.

value.rationale: The update is a standard and widely useful rectangular completion rule for finite relations. Exact graph-dependent completion time and sharp two-shore optimal round budget answer a natural closure-algorithm question, while the edge-arrival profile quantifies the most delayed instance. The comparison with the existing anchored recurrence makes the choice between two natural strategies quantitatively nontrivial: linear versus logarithmic worst-case parallel rounds. This is a motivated exact complexity invariant rather than an arbitrary finite example; it does not assert broader algorithmic hardness.
